name: 3 John
author: The writer calls himself simply "the elder," a title for a respected older leader who cared for a group of churches. Since early times Christians have identified him as John, one of Jesus' twelve disciples and a former fisherman from Galilee, who is said to have spent his later years in Ephesus. Some scholars think the elder was a different leader, sometimes called John the Elder, who belonged to the same circle of churches. The letter shares its style and outlook with 1 and 2 John, and most readers see one hand behind all three.
audience: This is a short personal letter to one man, Gaius, a believer the elder loved and trusted. He was part of a local church, probably in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey), that met in a home. The elder had heard good reports of how Gaius welcomed and cared for visiting Christian workers.
era: The letter is usually dated to the late first century AD, perhaps around AD 90, when the Roman Empire ruled the Mediterranean world. Most churches were small groups meeting in private houses, and travelling preachers and teachers moved between them. With no church buildings or salaries, these travellers depended on believers to give them food, lodging and help for the next stage of their journey. Letters were carried by hand, often by a trusted traveller who could add news in person.

notes.1:5: Gaius had been housing travelling Christian workers who refused support from non-believers, and some had returned to report his kindness to the elder's church.
notes.1:9: This answers trouble from Diotrephes, a local church leader who rejected the elder's earlier letter, refused his messengers, and expelled members who welcomed them.
notes.1:12: Demetrius, whom the elder commends, was probably the one carrying this letter to Gaius.
